Statistics for Normal People

What to think of the “data-driven” world

Preface

This is meant to be an easy-ish read for anyone curious about what “data-driven” actually means. Honestly, it doesn’t mean much. It’s an entire group of things. It’s anything having to do with drawing conclusions based on data. We can safely assume that just means statistics.

We’ll discuss the role of data in society in general, but there are two problems I want to explicitly address in this post. I contextualize and outline them here.

Problem 1: We don’t know what statistics is

My first goal is to explain why you should care. This isn’t about how… But why would any normal person care about stats? What even is stats?

And here’s what I mean by “normal person”. Normal people don’t know what a dot product is.

Normal people don’t really need evidence when they make a claim. That might sound crazy, but not when a claim is as something as trivial as “I had pancakes for breakfast” or “I don’t like eggs”.

You don’t need evidence for those claims, let alone “mathematical” evidence. And you shouldn’t. Evidence or proof doesn’t have a place in a conversation with your mom. Or a conversation with a friend. But it still has a place.

So when do we need evidence? Maybe if you skip a final exam for a funeral, your professor would want to see the death certificate. If I tell you “all Chinese people are three feet tall”, you’d want to see some evidence.

In research, you want to make some new claims based on science. You make a claim in an abstract. And you spend the rest of the 8 pages justifying it: what the context is, why you asked a specific question, and most importantly, how you got there. Doing some stats is almost always included in a full paper. That’s the “how we got there”. That’s the evidence. It’s proof. Statistics is becoming the standard for scientific proof.

Problem 2: It’s hard to interpret statistics as evidence

In the news you hear that…

That’s an issue. When you’re reading stats from the source, it’s always shrounded in a bunch of jargon. Even the most BASIC stats work has this entire suite of nonsense vocabulary you need to pretend to understand. Someone who’s taken an entire semester of a basic statistics class, and even excelled in it, could not explain to you what a p-value is. And those appear EVERYWHERE.

That makes statistics unreadable and uninterpretable

And that isn’t fair. We want to live in a democratic society. And when scientific proof is gatekept by math that you’re told is too complicated for you, that sucks. The moment math steps in, you’re frozen out of the conversation. It becomes difficult to have any opinion some mega genius math guy couldn’t just drown out with a bunch of random jargon and make you feel stupid for.

But here’s the thing, is that a lot of people who do the stats (and even know the jargon!) are just flat out lying. I’m going to show that to you.

And look, this just isn’t the point of science if you can’t understand it. Science is meant to be a collective effort to find the truth. Everyone should have a say. Even “non-experts”. Science isn’t supposed to abuse the prestige of math in order to freeze you out of the conversation, to make it harder to criticize or even distract from the science just being… bad.

Learning Objective

From our two problems, naturally two questions arise. By the end of reading this, we should be able to answer both:

“What is statistics?” and “Why does it help us draw conclusions?”

Structure

The first three sections are the easiest to read. And if you can understand them, then you can read the final two sections, which are the only ones with sub-sections.

TL;DR

We have a couple of problems:
1. We don’t know what statistics is.
2. It’s hard to interpret statistics as evidence.

So we naturally ask the questions:
“What is stats?”” and “Why does it help us draw conclusions?”

By the end, you should know:
What statistics is and how much we can trust it.

1. Defining Stats

Statistics is doing math with data.

2. A little hypothetical

In math, you can make conclusions and find “solutions”. So when data reflects reality, that means our mathematical conclusions are reality conclusions.

Basically we can use math on real life when real life is numbers.

If the idea of using math on real life is still too confusing, then here’s a hypothetical for you. I just asked you to sign a sheet of paper and you did it without reading it. Oops. Now you’re in a contract with me, starting this instant.

As part of the contract I’m giving you two apples every single day.

I hand you the first two apples. But you’re scared. How many apples will you have tomorrow? I guess just two more. But what about three days from now? Or 48 days from now? It’s scary not knowing.

\[2(\text{n}) = (\text{Count of Apples on Day n})\]

What we’ve done is created a “model” of this contract using math.

The math itself here is actually easy. The difficult part is actually conceptual.

3. What our hypothetical teaches us

What’s going on is that we can do math on numbers to study how they work. And if we can turn the real world into numbers, we can do math on them to see how the real world works.

Basically, we can do math on the world when it comes in numbers. Trusting the “conclusions” is just trusting math.

4. How we draw conclusions with statistics

So we can do math on the real world’s numbers to explain the real world.

But now how about a real world example? Nobody is in a contract to get apples.

So here is some real world data. We’ll call this the “tips” dataset. For now it should just just exist floating around in the ether. But here’s a sneak peak of it:

(244, 7)

This is the result of some code we ran. I won’t show the code because that would get a little confusing. But trust me, I ran it. And this is the result.

How we read this is that the dataset called “tips” has 244 (two hundred and forty four) rows, and 7 (seven) different columns.

That’s a grid. So the “tips” data is really just a spreadsheet.

4.1 Doing the statistics

Now let’s dive in. Let’s walk through performing our first statistical analysis! Trust me, this is easy. We’re going to start with finding the average. Specifically, the average number of

I’m going to run some code which will do math on the data. And I’ll show you the output here:

<Running code on the data to find the mean>
3.0

We’ve just performed math on data! We’ve just done statistics. Here’s the actual mathematical formula we just used:

\[\frac{1}{n}\Sigma_{i=1}^n(x_i)\]

This looks nothing like the apple equation we looked at. You do not need to understand this. Honestly, don’t even try. You can just appreciate how cool the symbols look. But this is the formula we just applied on our data in order to “do statistics”. The statistic we just found is called the “mean” (that’s a fancy word for average).

4.2 Drawing our conclusions

We can make a basic conclusion. We did math on the data to find the “mean” tip. Now we can conclude:

If you work at that restaurant, the average tip you’ll get is 3 dollars.

There is no math in that sentence. We have successfully used math to make a non-math conclusion! And that conclusion says something about reality.

We can take it one step further. There’s a column in the data called “sex”, the gender of the tipper. The person who gave the tip.

A genuinely interesting question I have is do men tip better than women? Generally the income of men is higher. And men are more likely to flirt with their server, maybe by tipping them more. These are just guesses but let’s see. We can just do the average twice, one for women and once for men.

<Running code on the data to find both means>
On average, men tip 3.09
On average, women tip 2.83

Wow. This is interesting. You can probably interpret these numbers yourself. But in any case, what we’ve just done is performed math again on numbers representing the real world. And now we can conclude:

Men are tipping more than women in the restaurant

5. The limitations of statistics

In this section I’m going to be covering what usually goes wrong with statistical analysis, and how you can spot it yourself.

But first of all, I want to apologize, because I lied to you. I told you that trusting statistics is just “trusting math”. But that isn’t true. The math isn’t the only thing we need to trust. If statistics is math with data, we can’t just trust the math. We need to trust the data as well.

\[\text{All errors in statistics come from data, not the math we do with it.}\]

Read the text above. This is the key takeaway. The math can basically never be wrong. So almost always, the mistakes we make with statistics is the numbers we chose to trust, not the math we do with those numbers.

If that makes sense, here’s some more explanation.

Remember that to make conclusions, we assume that the data reflects reality. We need to trust the data. But unfortunately, most of the time we can’t actually “just trust the data”. At least not blindly. If you are standing in front of me and I have a measuring tape, I could easily measure your height. I would probably place that little metal tab under your feet and then stretch the tape up to your head. Say I measured you to be 5’8”, which is 68 inches.

5.1 When the data is wrong

That’s just one way we can turn reality into numbers. In a statistical environment we call that data. I would’ve just collected data on your height. You’d probably trust the data if you trust me. I mean measuring somebody’s height is relatively straight forward. But you can’t trust just anybody.

For example, here’s something that happens all the time in real life. Universities are the main organizations that publish research. Large companies do this too. Those are called “white papers”, but they aren’t open like universities. If a company does their own research, they don’t really have a reason to publish the results to the public. Or even to people who pay to see research. To them, their conclusions are the property of their company.

But anyways, universities publish a lot of research. And so they often need access to people they can survey. The easiest people to survey are often people at the university. Those are the students.

But here is the issue, is that the group of people who were surveyed is the students. But they frame their research in a way that suggests that data collected from them are representative of all people. For example, say they survey 18 people to see if a new kind of of artificial sweetener they developed is better than sugar. Those 18 people will all be college-age American results. And the entire world is not mostly college-age American adults. What if it turns out that older adults have eaten less artificial sweeteners in their lifetime. And it turns out that if you surveyed older people, they would say the sweetener is a 3/10 on average because they’re less used to the taste. As opposed to the survey group, which gave a 5/10.

This is just an example. But this happens all the time.

5.2 Why sometimes that doesn’t really matter (the purpose of stats is to use it)

Small surveys are still useful, though.

If you had to survey 3,000 to represent the entire world for a small paper then nothing would get published. Small surveys are great for a “pilot study”. That’s like how when a TV show is about to get made, they create a pilot episode to show producers to pitch the idea. Then those guys decide if the show gets made. Most of the time a show doesn’t make it past the first pilot episode.

Studies do this too. They do a small study to demonstrate their point before they have funding to do it on a bunch of people, or just to test some smaller conclusion out.

5.3 Why it’s hard to admit the data is wrong (there’s an inside-issue with science)

We’ve covered what happens when the statistics are interesting or particularly useful, but what if they aren’t? And that certainly can happen.

Here’s an example.

Publishing null results is science. But they’re not as interesting. And while research isn’t driven by money like businesses are, all of these publishers strive for relevance in the scientific community. They publish the most interesting findings. And because null results aren’t very interesting, researchers will just design their own statistical test just for their own study that will give them results they want.1

Conclusion

Now you’ve seen some stats in action, and I’ve taught you how to identify mistakes scientists make.2

The most common mistakes are:

  • When the data is wrong and we don’t know
  • When the data is wrong and we don’t admit
  • When we pretend like statistics isn’t just doing math

On that last one, notice how all the conclusions we drew were “scoped”. We only made conclusions about the server’s at THAT specific restaurant which produced the data. And that’s how all of this works. If you ask five people what their favorite color is, they might all say blue. But you can’t say that everyone’s favorite color is blue. That’s just wrong.

You can basically never say anything conclusive from a single statistical test. And if you try and do that, it’s not just irresponsible as a scientist. You’re just a liar. People might not trust you, but they trust science. So when make some claim like “all Chinese people are two feet tall” and then write a whole paper about it with a bunch of equations, people assume that you’re being as honest as science.

A lot of people are just using stats to wrongly interpret the data. Or they just form a conclusion. And do the stats performatively to manufacture evidence for a claim they never had any interest in questioning in the first place. Then they draw make conclusions that they literally cannot.

I mean technically you can “conclude” whatever you want to as a human being. If I see it’s raining out I can “conclude” that it will never stop raining ever. That’s not scientific. But that makes sense. Nobody is perfect. We all say things we shouldn’t.

We lie and cheat and steal all the time as human beings. We say mean things. Or maybe you eat somebody else’s lunch from the fridge. Statistics is no different. It’s just another thing you can lie and cheat and steal with. So when you see somebody do math with data, you don’t need to question the math. Question what they’re saying with it.

Footnotes

  1. This is called “p-hacking”. Earlier I said that something called “p-values” appear in research papers all the time. They’re part of a statistics method. Generally, the lower they are, the more “significant” they are (read as interesting). So researchers do a bunch of statistical tests and pick the one with the lowest (most interesting) p-value to include in their paper.↩︎

  2. I am not exaggerating when I say this basically covers everything. Almost all mistakes with statistics are just these things at larger scale and in different math equations that are beyond the scope of this post.↩︎
